content.comment_body: Hello, I read in this forum that using cursor keys usually requires pressing ESC, but then I found a video online ([url]) showing it can be done differently. Can someone provide an example?

Welcome to the forum. There are two main functions for the cursor keys: system functions and operations within the [product_name] program. For system tasks, ESC is not needed, like scrolling between activated messages or adjusting parameters and menus. If you want to trigger a function within the [product_name] program (for example, switching on a motor with the cursor key), you need to press ESC and the cursor key together.

Could someone share an example? I tried using an editable parameter (such as on-delay time) on the [product_name] display, but the cursor keys don't operate as expected. When I press the down arrow, it shows the date and time and cycles through inputs, outputs, and other screens.

You need to include the parameters you want to change within a message screen. Select the desired message, then hold ESC for more than two seconds. A black bar will appear in an input/output field. Use the cursor up/down to navigate fields. Once the field is selected, press OK (Enter) on the [product_name] display. The bar becomes a blinking box; you can now change values with cursor up/down and move position with left/right. Press OK again to finish and return. Use cursor keys to move to another field or ESC to exit.
Thanks, that clarified things. Is there a way to disable this menu entirely so that the end user can't access it?
You can set protection for message screens and the blocks whose parameters you display in the message. This limits user access to specific edits.
I'm referring to the menu starting with date and time, then showing multiple pages with settings like '[product_name] Select, [product_name] Settings', etc.

If that's the menu you mean, it can't be fully locked. You can switch from administrator to operator mode, which reduces what can be changed in the main menu. For example, the IP address can then only be viewed, not edited.

The only guaranteed way to fully secure a [product_name] display is to use a physical solution, such as an acrylic cover with a key switch. For restricting access to parameters shown in messages, you can use a digital input for service mode (such as I8 or I16). Only when this input is active will the service messages show, allowing authorized changes.
When you add several screens to the project and activate them simultaneously, the one with the highest priority is displayed. To see other screens, use the up/down cursor keys—no ESC key is required.

analysis.insight_summary: Forum users find the navigation logic for cursor keys with [product_name] displays and controllers unintuitive, especially where system functions differ from programmed actions requiring ESC plus cursor keys. There is concern about restricting end-user access to system menus; while partial limitation is possible through user mode settings or physical methods, full menu locking via software is unavailable.
analysis.user_expectations: Users want straightforward cursor navigation for editing parameters, without needing to use extra key combinations. They also seek a reliable method to prevent end-users from accessing system menus, preferably with a software solution.
